summary: Defines how the entities in a Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain, the mobile access gateway and the local mobility anchor, interact with an AAA server using Diameter. The main use is downloading and updating per-device policy profiles from a remote policy store. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Network helpers keep asking a central office for each visitor's rulebook, and the office can send updated rules whenever they change.

subtitle: How Proxy Mobile IPv6 gateways and anchors fetch and update device policy from a Diameter server.

tldr.problem: In a Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain, each mobile node needs a policy profile, and keeping those profiles on every gateway does not scale for large deployments.
tldr.mechanism: The Mobile Access Gateway and the Local Mobility Anchor talk Diameter to a home AAA server that doubles as a remote policy store, using a few new and reused AVPs on existing Diameter applications.
tldr.outcome: Profiles can be downloaded and updated centrally, PBUs can be authorized, and addresses can be assigned or recorded by the AAA server.

today: RFC 5779 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This specification defines Authentication, Authorization and Accounting (AAA) interactions between a Mobile Access Gateway (MAG) and a AAA server, and between a Local Mobility Anchor (LMA) and a AAA server, inside a Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) domain defined in RFC 5213. They are primarily used to download and update mobile node (MN) specific policy profile information held in a remote policy store.

Downloading profiles from a remote store eases deployment and maintenance of larger PMIPv6 domains. The same AAA infrastructure that authenticates the MN for network access can deliver some or all of the profile to the MAG. Once the MN is authenticated, the MAG sends a Proxy Binding Update (PBU) to the LMA, which may authorize it against the AAA infrastructure.

The home AAA (HAAA) server is co-located with the remote policy store. The protocol is Diameter, from RFC 3588.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every door guard memorizing every visitor's rules, they look the rules up at one central office using the same system that checks visitors in.

sections.title: Solution Overview
sections.content:
The document defines Diameter interactions between the MAG and the HAAA, and between the LMA and the HAAA. The policy profile is downloaded from the HAAA to the MAG when the MN attaches to the domain.

On attachment, network access authentication usually starts, possibly based on EAP. The MAG, acting as a Network Access Server (NAS), queries the HAAA over Diameter. If the HAAA finds the subscriber is also authorized for PMIPv6, PMIPv6 specific information is returned with the successful authentication answer.

After authentication, the MAG sends a PBU to the LMA based on the profile. The LMA then interacts with the HAAA to fetch the relevant parts of the profile and authorization information for the mobility session. The HAAA is the PMIPv6 remote policy store.
sections.plainLanguage: First the visitor is checked in at the door. Then the door guard tells the building's main desk, and the main desk checks the rules with the central office too.

sections.title: MAG and LMA Interfaces
sections.content:
No new Application-IDs or Command Codes are defined. The specification is generic to any Diameter application suited to network access authentication and authorization, such as NASREQ (RFC 4005) and EAP (RFC 4072).

On the MAG-to-HAAA interface, the MAG is a Diameter client used to bootstrap the mobility session. The User-Name AVP SHOULD carry the MN identity in Network Access Identifier (NAI) format unless it is suppressed, for example by identity hiding. At minimum the MN's home realm MUST be available so the request can be routed to the right HAAA.

The LMA-to-HAAA interface is used to authorize the incoming PBU, update the HAAA with the LMA address, delegate assignment of the MN home network prefix (MN-HNP) or IPv4 home address to the HAAA, and for accounting and session management. The Auth-Request-Type AVP MUST be set to AUTHORIZE_ONLY. If the HAAA cannot authorize the session, it MUST reply with DIAMETER_AUTHORIZATION_REJECTED (5003), and the PBU is rejected with an error in the PBA sent to the MAG.

Authorization MUST be performed at least for the initial PBU. For later re-registration and handover PBUs it MAY be repeated.
sections.plainLanguage: The door guard and the main desk each have their own line to the central office. The main desk must get a yes from the office for a new visitor, and a no means the visitor is turned away.

sections.title: Attribute Value Pairs
sections.content:
Diameter carries information in Attribute Value Pairs (AVPs). This RFC defines four new AVPs and reuses others:

  • PMIP6-IPv4-Home-Address (code 505): an IPv4 address for the MN, used on both interfaces.
  • PMIP6-DHCP-Server-Address (code 504): the address of the DHCP server assigned to the MAG.
  • Mobile-Node-Identifier (code 506): an NAI-format identity the MAG can use in later PBU and PBA exchanges, for example when identity hiding applies.
  • Service-Configuration (code 507): a grouped AVP pairing a service and an LMA.

The MIP6-Agent-Info grouped AVP (code 486, from RFC 5447) is extended with PMIP6-IPv4-Home-Address. It carries the LMA address and the MN home prefix. If the LMA delegates address assignment, it sends all zeroes (0::0 or 0.0.0.0) and the HAAA returns the assigned value. The low 64 bits of a MIP6-Home-Link-Prefix (code 125) MUST be all zeroes.

Calling-Station-Id (code 31) carries the link-layer identifier, written in upper-case ASCII with octets separated by a hyphen, for example 00-23-32-C9-79-38. Service-Selection (code 493) carries a service identifier that MUST be unique within the PMIPv6 domain. The IANA section registers codes 504 to 507.
sections.plainLanguage: AVPs are labeled boxes of information in a message. Some boxes hold an address, some a visitor's name, and some a service and the desk that offers it.

sections.title: Capability Bits
sections.content:
The MIP6-Feature-Vector AVP, from RFC 5447, gets three new capability flag bits. Because both sides announce capabilities, a capability that both announce is known to be mutually supported. The LMA-to-HAAA interface defines no new capability values.

  • PMIP6_SUPPORTED means the sender supports PMIPv6. It can also allow PMIPv6 mobility per subscription.
  • IP4_HOA_SUPPORTED means IPv4 home address assignment is supported. If the HAAA leaves it unset, it does not authorize IPv4 address configuration.
  • LOCAL_MAG_ROUTING_SUPPORTED means direct routing between MNs anchored to the same MAG is supported, without tunneling via the LMA. If the HAAA clears it, direct routing is not authorized.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side holds up cards showing what it can do. Only the tricks both sides show are used.

sections.title: Session Management
sections.content:
The HAAA, MAG and LMA Diameter entities SHOULD be stateful and keep the Authorization Session State Machine from RFC 3588. If state is kept, a PMIPv6 mobility session identified by any of the Binding Cache Entry lookup keys of RFC 5213 MUST map to a single Diameter Session-Id. When both interfaces are used with state, one mobility session has two distinct Diameter sessions on the HAAA, and the HAAA SHOULD allow that.

Existing Diameter commands handle termination. The LMA or MAG MAY send a Session-Termination-Request (STR), answered by the HAAA with a Session-Termination-Answer (STA). The HAAA MAY send an Abort-Session-Request (ASR) to the LMA or MAG, which acknowledge with an Abort-Session-Answer (ASA). The actual PMIPv6 termination happens at the PMIPv6 protocol level.
sections.plainLanguage: The offices keep a notebook entry for each visitor. Either side can say the visit is ending, and the central office can also tell a guard to end one.

sections.title: Example Signaling Flow
sections.content:
The RFC's example shows PMIPv6 bootstrapping in two steps. In step 1 the MN is authenticated with EAP, and the MAG talks to the HAAA with the Diameter EAP application. The MAG-to-HAAA AVPs appear only in the Diameter EAP Request (DER) that starts the exchange and in the Diameter EAP Answer (DEA) that completes it successfully.

In step 2 the MAG sends a PBU to the LMA. The LMA uses the Diameter NASREQ application (an AA-Request and AA-Answer) to authorize the MN and to update the HAAA with the assigned LMA information. This step may also help assign the MN-HNP. Then the LMA returns a PBA and the PMIPv6 tunnel comes up.
sections.plainLanguage: First the visitor proves who they are. Then the main desk gets approval from the central office, and only then is the visitor's path opened.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations of the Diameter base protocol, the Diameter EAP application, the Diameter NASREQ application and Diameter Mobile IPv6 bootstrapping (RFC 5447) apply. Messages between the LMA and the Diameter server may pass through AAA brokers or Diameter agents such as proxies. In that case the communication relies on the security properties of those intermediaries.
sections.plainLanguage: If notes pass through other helpers on the way to the central office, you have to trust those helpers too.
